title: Transfer functions, voltage and current gain, transimpedance

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
A **transfer function** is the ratio of an output phasor to an input phasor at a given frequency. Its units tell you what kind of gain it is: volts over volts is a **voltage gain**, amps over amps is a **current gain**, volts over amps (ohms) is a **transimpedance**, and amps over volts (siemens) is a **transconductance**.

Amplifiers are described the same way. A real amplifier has an input resistance, an output resistance and a controlled source. Connecting a source and a load creates voltage dividers at both ports, so the overall gain is less than the intrinsic gain. Good voltage amplifiers have large \(R_{in}\) and small \(R_{out}\).

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ H(j\omega) = \frac{Y(j\omega)}{X(j\omega)} \]
Voltage amplifier with source resistance \(R_s\) and load \(R_L\):
\[ \frac{v_o}{v_s} = \frac{R_{in}}{R_{in} + R_s}\cdot A_v \cdot \frac{R_L}{R_L + R_{out}} \]
Gain in decibels: \(20\log_{10}|H|\) for voltage or current ratios.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
An amplifier has \(R_{in} = 50\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(A_v = 40\), \(R_{out} = 200\ \Omega\). It is driven from a source with \(R_s = 10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and drives \(R_L = 800\ \Omega\).
\[ \frac{v_o}{v_s} = \frac{50}{60}\cdot 40\cdot\frac{800}{1000} = 0.833 \cdot 40 \cdot 0.8 \approx 26.7 \]
That is \(20\log_{10}26.7 \approx 28.5\) dB, down from the intrinsic 32 dB.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Using \(10\log_{10}\) for a voltage ratio. That is for power ratios.
- Forgetting the input divider when the source has internal resistance.
- Mixing up transimpedance (Ω) and transconductance (S).
- Thinking a dB value can only be positive. Attenuation gives negative dB.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Transfer functions are the common currency of the rest of the course. Pole–zero analysis, Bode plots, feedback block diagrams and op-amp models are all built from them, and the loading formula above is the first step toward two-port models and feedback impedance.
